member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Network.CompressorStationPlanner
member.summary:
Answers "how many compressor stations, and how far apart?" for a route with a real elevation profile.
The planner owns the physics (pipe-flow model, flowing temperature, gas) and three building blocks shared by every placement method: - marching along the route, forward from A or backward from B, stopping where the pressure reaches a given value (located exactly by Brent's method inside a step); - : the hydraulics of any given layout (station positions and discharge pressures), which optimisation methods use to score candidates; - the result assembly (sections, friction / elevation split, isentropic power per station).
Placement methods: (method 1) and (method 2); tabulates power against the number of stations.
Stated assumptions: - pipe flow is isothermal at the flowing (ground) temperature; the gas leaves each station cooled to that temperature (aftercooler duty is not computed here); - station power is the isentropic power (η = 1) from the fluid's heat-capacity ratio: the minimum any machine needs. Real power follows from the hardware chosen later.

member.summary:
Velocity and erosional ratio at every segment end of a section; the maxima are stored on the section and checked against the criteria.
Density at a segment end: ρ = ρ̄·P/P̄, i.e. the segment's average Z is kept over the segment (ρ = P·M/(Z·R·T)). Over a marching step (≤ 1 km by default) Z changes by well under 0.1 %, so this error is negligible against the velocity limits being checked. The segment inlet is covered by the previous segment's end, and the section inlet is the highest-pressure (lowest-velocity) point, so ends suffice.
Assembles a plan. has one entry more than (A → first station, …, last station → B).

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Network.NetworkSolver
member.summary:
Steady-state solution of a gas network by the nodal method: unknowns are the pressures of the fixed-flow nodes, equations are the mass balances Σ inflow − Σ outflow − withdrawal = 0 at those nodes. Solved by Newton's method with a central-difference Jacobian (each pipe flow depends only on its two end pressures) and a backtracking line search on the largest imbalance.
Pipe flows come from each pipe's , so any segment calculation can be used. Flow reversal is handled by solving the segment in the other direction (elevation change negated). Friction models that are undefined in the laminar–turbulent transition (Colebrook, Haaland, Swamee-Jain) can fail on nearly idle pipes of a loop; Churchill covers every regime.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Network.SegmentResult
member.summary:
State of one solved segment.
The total pressure drop is split into an elevation (hydrostatic) part and a friction part: ΔP_elevation = ρ_lm·g·Δz, ρ_lm = ρ̄·P_lm/P_avg, P_lm = (P1 − P2)/ln(P1/P2) ΔP_friction = ΔP_total − ΔP_elevation ρ̄ is the density at the solver's average pressure; scaling it to the log-mean pressure makes the elevation part exact for a static gas column at constant Z (P2 = P1·e^(−s/2)). The split is a definition for reporting: the momentum balance itself is integrated as a whole (P² form). Uphill ΔP_elevation > 0; downhill it is negative (the gas regains pressure).

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Network.MaximumSpacingPlacement
member.summary:
Method 1 — greedy maximum spacing (hydraulic marching).
1. start at A with the inlet pressure; 2. march along the route until the pressure falls to the minimum suction pressure; place a station there, which restores the discharge pressure; 3. repeat until B; 4. the last station discharges exactly what B needs (backward march from B). If the gas would arrive below the target without falling to the minimum suction, one more station is placed where the backward profile from B reaches the discharge pressure.
Gives the minimum number of stations for the pressure limits, with the terrain. It does not minimise power or cost, and the last station can be much smaller than the others (use ). See Edgar, Himmelblau & Bickel (SPE J. 18(2), 1978) for the cost-optimal problem.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Network.EqualRatioPlacement
member.summary:
Method 2 — N stations with equal pressure ratios.
Every station discharges at the station discharge pressure P_d and takes suction at a common pressure P_s, so every ratio is P_d / P_s: 1. the last station sits where the backward profile from B (at the delivery target) reaches P_d — its position does not depend on P_s; 2. P_s is the root (Brent's method) of g(P_s) = (position of the N-th point where the forward march from A, restarting at P_d after each station, falls to P_s) − (position of 1). Raising P_s brings the stations closer, so g decreases.
This is the usual industry heuristic. Equal ratios minimise compression energy for stations with the same suction temperature, but not total cost once station capital cost counts (Edgar, Himmelblau & Bickel 1978). N must be at least the count found by ; with fewer stations P_s would have to fall below the minimum suction.
